items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: My business partner and wife Lydia said, “Maybe you should have your own label.”

ctx.x: Oh! We can back up and go to the formation of Golden Beam.

Where did that come from... I had so many projects and I have loads and loads of archival tapes. My business partner and wife Lydia said, “Maybe you should have your own label.” Which at the time I naively didn’t know what that meant! Bless her. She went into this, having a label, because I’m more the artist, and she’s more pragmatic, “Who’s going to run this? Who’s going to operate this?” Got into, “If we’re going to have this label I don’t want to do all the work,” so we looked around for young people who could…

state and got into a zone, and did this music with the synthesizer and a resonating bell which I designed in co-partnership with the Sabian Cymbal Company. My son-in-law Ben Surman would produce this, Music In The Key Of Om. It subsequently got nominated for a Grammy and also my daughter Farah actually posed for the cover of that. That helped really give it a feel as to what the music was. So, after that I’d been listening to Foday Musa Suso, who is from Gambia living in the States, living in Chicago. He’d been…

items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: we helped him you know when they were having some financial problems, Lydia and I — or Lydia arranged and shall we say fundraised the concert.

ctx.x: You had an association with Karl Berger and the Creative Music Studio. Can you tell me how that came about and how you think about your contributions to that now, in retrospect?

I think Karl Berger, I think Ornette has something to do with that. I just came and did some teaching with the students. And then we had Dave Holland, we had Colin Wolcott, what’s his name — Trilok Gurtu So there were a lot of current musicians that were like on the faculty teaching there. And so you know the challenge was for us, when we first started, was to play — to get the musicians who were at different levels of being able to play. Some couldn’t even play scales. Some — and so we had to try to figure out a…

He said an interesting thing that, he said, “Playing free requires more discipline, more stringent than anybody can tell me from the outside. The more precise you get, the more free you are.” And I remember when he said that I just like — wow — that if you observe it and listen to it you may get the impression that people are just playing randomly and that’s not what he’s about at all.
